# The task model

Every task is modeled as a **game** that the participant is asked to play. A game is
described by five parts: its **game type**, its **game rules**, its **game
motivators**, its **game phases** and its **game facets**. This page defines each part,
says what else a model records, and works through examples. Every value named here is
defined on the [game vocabulary](tasks/vocabulary.md) page.

On this page the participant is called the **player** when the game is being described.

## Why a game

A task is something a person is asked to do, for a reason, under rules, with particular
material and equipment. That is also what a game is. Describing a task as a game asks
the same plain questions of every task: what kind of game is it, how is it played, why
does the player try, does it come in parts, and how is it delivered.

The answers come from closed lists, so they can be compared. The Stroop Color-Word Task
and the Eriksen Flanker Task turn out to be the same kind of game, with one rule
answered differently. Two experiments that both call themselves "Stroop" turn out to
differ in how the answer is given. A task with no standard name can still be described
completely. None of this can be read from a task name.

The model describes the task as designed: what the participant is asked to do. It does
not describe the events of any one run, which is what HED annotation does, and it does
not say which mental processes the task engages, which is the job of
[the cognitive process model](process_model.md).

## The five parts

| Part | The question it answers | How it is recorded |
|---|---|---|
| [Game type](#game-type) | What kind of game is the player playing? | One of ten types |
| [Game rules](#game-rules) | How is this game played? | Answers to the rule questions of the game type; only the answers that differ from the default are stated |
| [Game motivators](#game-motivators) | Why does the player try? | Answers to five questions, the same for every game type |
| [Game phases](#game-phases) | Does the game have parts beyond its own structure? | A list of phase names, usually empty |
| [Game facets](#game-facets) | How is the game delivered? | Values for nine facets, the same for every game type |

(game-type)=
### Game type

The game type says what the player is doing. There are ten, and every task has exactly
one. Each type has a sentence that tells it from the others, given in the "How to tell"
column: a task is of that type when the sentence is true of it.

```{include} _generated/game_types_table.md
```

The type is decided by what the player does and what is measured, not by the construct
the task is meant to study. The N-Back Task is used to study working memory, but the
player answers each item under a rule (does it match the one n back?), so it is a game
of responding under a rule, with a rule saying that something is held in mind. The Digit
Span Task also studies working memory, and it is a game of studying and then being
tested.

(game-rules)=
### Game rules

Each game type asks its own questions about how the game is played. Every question has
a **default answer**, the usual way that game is played, and a list of other answers. A
model states a rule only when its answer differs from the default, so a model that
states no rules plays its game in the default way, and the rules a model does state are
exactly what makes it distinctive.

```{include} _generated/game_rules_table.md
```

Five game types (Solve a puzzle, Make a movement, Find the way, Report on yourself and
Hold a state) have no rule questions yet. Few tasks in the catalog are of those types,
and a rule question is added only when it separates tasks that are actually there. As
more tasks are modeled those types are expected to gain rules.

Three tasks of one game type, respond under a rule, show how rules separate tasks:

- The **Stroop Color-Word Task** states one rule. *What competes with the correct
  response?* An `irrelevant_dimension`: the word, which the player must ignore.
- The **Eriksen Flanker Task** states the same rule with another answer:
  `neighbouring_items`, the flankers.
- The **Go/No-Go Task** leaves that rule at its default, `none`, and states a different
  one. *Must the player ever hold back?* `withhold_on_some`.

(game-motivators)=
### Game motivators

The motivators say why the player tries. There are five questions, the same for every
game type. The first is answered for every task. The other four are answered only when
something is won, lost or delivered.

```{include} _generated/game_motivators_table.md
```

The answers to the first question, `drive`, separate four situations that are easy to
confuse:

- `instructions_only` - the player tries because they were asked to. This is most
  tasks. The ordinary instruction "as fast and as accurately as you can" is this value.
- `reward_goal` - winning or avoiding a loss is what the game is about, as in the Iowa
  Gambling Task.
- `reward_stake` - a reward or loss is attached to doing well at a game that is about
  something else, as in the Monetary Incentive Delay Task, where money depends on how
  fast the player responds to a target.
- `unearned_outcome` - something pleasant or unpleasant is delivered whatever the
  player does, as in Pavlovian fear conditioning.
- `instructed_emphasis` - the instruction puts one of speed or accuracy first.

The motivators are not the cognitive processes of reward or motivation. They record
what the experimenter built into the game; what that engages in the player belongs to
the process model.

(game-phases)=
### Game phases

A phase is a named part of a game that a study reports separately, beyond the structure
its game type already has. A game of studying and then being tested already has a study
part and a test part, and those are not listed as phases. Phases are listed when the
same game is played through distinct stages, as when a relation is learned and then
withdrawn.

```{include} _generated/game_phases_table.md
```

Most tasks name no phase. The Pavlovian Fear Conditioning Task names `acquisition` and
`extinction`; the Probabilistic Selection Task names `acquisition` and `transfer`.
The list of phases is short because it has been drawn from the traditional tasks alone.
Modeling the tasks of individual papers, which have practice blocks and multi-part
sessions, is expected to show whether more is needed.

(game-facets)=
### Game facets

The facets say how the game is delivered: what the player perceives, what equipment is
used, how the trials are run, and who the players are. There are nine, the same for
every game type. A facet lists the values that are present, and a facet with nothing to
say is left out; there are no "none" values.

```{include} _generated/game_facets_table.md
```

Every facet value corresponds to HED tags, listed with the value on the
[game vocabulary](tasks/vocabulary.md) page: the stimulus modality `visual` is the tag
`Visual-presentation`, the stimulus type `words` is `Word`, the task I/O device
`microphone` is `Microphone`. Where no exact tag exists the vocabulary gives the
nearest one and says so. The facets are where a task model meets the HED annotation of
the events of a run.

## What else a model records

Three more things complete the description of a game. They are not classification axes
but they are needed to compare two tasks or to rebuild one.

- **Settings** name the quantities a study chooses when it runs the game: a retention
  interval, a set size, the proportion of congruent trials. The model of a task in the
  catalog lists the names of the settings that studies vary, with no numbers, because
  the numbers differ from study to study. The model of the task in one paper gives the
  values.
- **Material** is one sentence saying what the stimuli are: "Color words (RED, BLUE)
  printed in ink of a matching or a different color."
- **Combined games.** Some tasks give the player a second job. It is recorded as a
  second game, with its own game type, and the way the two are combined: in quick
  succession, throughout, interleaved, inserted or chained. The main game is the one the
  task's measure comes from. Holding the eyes on a fixation point while a cueing task
  is played is the Fixate Task combined `throughout`; verifying an equation between the
  items of a memory list, in the Operation Span Task, is a game of responding under a
  rule combined `interleaved`.

## The standard form and its variants

A named task is not one game but a small family of them. The model of a catalog task
therefore describes one **standard form**, the form that the task's inclusion test
defines, and then lists its **variants**: the other forms that whole studies run. A
variant states only what differs from the standard form, in the same terms, and inherits
the rest.

Three variants of the Stroop Color-Word Task, as the catalog records them:

- **Manual (Button-Press) Stroop** changes one facet: the task I/O device becomes a
  computer screen and a keyboard. The ink color is reported by key press instead of
  aloud.
- **Counting Stroop** changes one rule: the rule asks the player to `count`. A number
  word is printed one to four times and the player reports how many words there are.
- **Face-Word Stroop** changes four facets and adds two cognitive processes. An emotion
  word is written across an expressive face and the player names the expression.

Not every difference between two studies is a variant. A factor that one study varies
(congruent against incongruent trials) is a manipulation, and a part that some studies
add is an optional step of the procedure; both are recorded in the task's inclusion
test. The rules are in
[Task facets and variants](methods/task_criteria/04_task_facets_and_variants.md).

## Worked examples

### One rule: the Stroop Color-Word Task

- **Game type:** Respond under a rule. The answer depends only on the stimulus in front
  of the player and the rule: name the ink color.
- **Game rules:** one stated. *What competes with the correct response?*
  `irrelevant_dimension`. Every other rule takes its default: no cue, nothing held in
  mind, a response on every trial, the rule is instructed and does not change.
- **Game motivators:** `drive` is `instructions_only`.
- **Game phases:** none.
- **Game facets:** stimulus modality `visual`; stimulus type `words`; task I/O device
  `computer_screen` and `microphone`; trial structure `fixed_time_trials`; population
  `young_adults`.
- **Settings:** `proportion_congruent`. **Material:** color words printed in ink of a
  matching or a different color.

### Motivators and phases: the Pavlovian Fear Conditioning Task

- **Game type:** Watch or listen. No answer is scored against a correct one; the
  measure is the response to the stream itself.
- **Game rules:** one stated. *What is the player told to do while it runs?* `none`.
- **Game motivators:** `drive` is `unearned_outcome`; `sign` is `loss`; `earned_by` is
  `nothing`; `what` is `aversive`; `real` is `paid`. The shock comes whatever the player
  does.
- **Game phases:** `acquisition`, then `extinction`.
- **Game facets:** stimulus modality `visual` and `somatic`; stimulus type `shapes` and
  `electrical`; emotional aspect `emotion_induction`; task I/O device `computer_screen`;
  trial structure `fixed_time_trials`; population `young_adults`.

### A game about winning: the Iowa Gambling Task

- **Game type:** Choose for a payoff. No option is correct by instruction; the decks
  differ in what they pay.
- **Game rules:** none stated. It is the default game of its type: several options with
  hidden payoffs, learned by trying them, trading the amount won against the risk of
  loss.
- **Game motivators:** `drive` is `reward_goal`; `sign` is `both`; `earned_by` is
  `choice`; `what` is `money`; `real` is `paid` or `hypothetical`, because the task is
  commonly run both ways.
- **Game phases:** none.
- **Game facets:** stimulus modality `visual`; stimulus type `value_amounts` and
  `game_objects`; task I/O device `keyboard` and `computer_screen`; trial structure
  `self_paced_trials`; feedback `trial_feedback`; population `young_adults`.

### A second game: the Operation Span Task

- **Game type:** Study, then be tested.
- **Game rules:** four stated. The studied material is a `sequence_order`; it is held
  for `seconds`; the interval is filled by a `distraction`; the test is `serial_recall`.
- **Game motivators:** `drive` is `instructions_only`.
- **Combined with:** a game of responding under a rule, `interleaved`: an equation is
  verified between each item to be remembered.

## Comparing tasks

Because every model answers the same questions, two tasks are compared by laying their
answers side by side. Three tasks of the catalog, in their standard forms:

| Part | Stroop Color-Word | Eriksen Flanker | Go/No-Go |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game type | Respond under a rule | Respond under a rule | Respond under a rule |
| Rule: what competes? | `irrelevant_dimension` | `neighbouring_items` | `none` (default) |
| Rule: must the player hold back? | `always_respond` (default) | `always_respond` (default) | `withhold_on_some` |
| Motivators: drive | `instructions_only` | `instructions_only` | `instructions_only` |
| Phases | none | none | none |
| Facet: stimulus modality | `visual` | `visual` | `visual` |
| Facet: stimulus type | `words` | `symbols` | `letters` |
| Facet: task I/O device | `computer_screen`, `microphone` | `computer_screen`, `button_box` | `computer_screen`, `keyboard` |
| Facet: trial structure | `fixed_time_trials` | `fixed_time_trials` | `fixed_time_trials` |

The three are the same kind of game, motivated and delivered in much the same way. What
separates them is one rule each, and the table says which. The same comparison can be
made between a catalog task and the task in a paper, or between two papers, and it is
what the listings [tasks by game type](tasks/by_game_type.md) and
[tasks by facet](tasks/by_facet.md) are built from.

## What the vocabulary does not yet say

The vocabulary is deliberately small. A value is generally admitted when two or more tasks need
it; a value that only one task needs is written as a note on that task and kept in a
register of candidates (`data/vocabulary_candidates.json` in the
[repository](https://github.com/hed-standard/hed-task)), where it waits for a second
use. The vocabulary was drawn from the traditional tasks of the catalog, so it is
expected to grow as the tasks of papers and datasets are modeled, and
[The modeling process](modeling_process.md) says how a missing value is recorded.
